vignette: Lena, a 20-year-old South Eastern Asian woman married to another soldier, has been struggling with the aftermath of an assault that occurred several months ago. The traumatic event was a violent attack at a local bar where Lena had gone to celebrate her friend's promotion. The memory of that night is still vivid and fragmented, mostly visual images that she struggles to reconcile with reality. On that fateful evening, Lena found herself in the midst of an altercation between two groups of soldiers. Suddenly, she was pulled aside by one of the aggressors who proceeded to physically assault her. Despite her attempts to break free, she felt utterly powerless as he pushed her against a wall and threatened her. The memory is still so extreme that it feels almost surreal, like something that could not possibly have happened to her. Since then, Lena has developed several maladaptive strategies to cope with the distressing memories. She overeats frequently, finding solace in food as a way to distract herself from the overwhelming feelings of fear and helplessness. This behavior has led to significant weight gain, which only adds to her sense of unrecognizability. In addition to eating more than usual, Lena often redirects her thoughts by focusing on other activities or memories, trying to push away the traumatic images that keep resurfacing. She also spends considerable time overanalyzing the details of the assault, attempting to make sense of how she could have prevented it from happening. Lena's memory of the event feels alien, as though it belongs to someone else rather than herself. The visual nature of her memories is particularly distressing, and they often intrude upon her daily life without warning. These intrusive images are so vivid that Lena finds herself feeling detached from reality, unable to fully trust what she sees or experiences. The assault has significantly impacted Lena’s sense of self and her connection to the military community. She feels as though others would have been able to stop the event from happening if they had intervened. This belief has led her to feel increasingly isolated within her unit, where once she felt a strong sense of camaraderie. The assault has also disrupted her cultural ties, leaving her feeling disconnected from her South Eastern Asian heritage and the community that once provided her with support and identity. Over time, Lena's avoidance behaviors have become more pronounced. She avoids going out in public alone or visiting places where similar altercations could occur, limiting her social interactions and activities. This avoidance has strained her marriage, as she is often reluctant to participate in events or outings with her husband and his colleagues. Her occupational performance has also been affected; Lena finds it difficult to focus on training exercises and mission planning because the memories of the assault frequently resurface. What frightens Lena most is not just the memory itself but the fear that such an event could happen again, leaving her feeling constantly vigilant and hypervigilant in situations that once felt safe. She has begun to withdraw from many aspects of her life, isolating herself further and deepening her sense of unrecognizability. It was only after a particularly distressing incident where Lena experienced flashbacks during a training exercise, causing her to become physically ill, that she realized she needed help. The overwhelming nature of these symptoms finally compelled her to seek psychological support, hoping that through therapy, she could regain control over her life and reclaim the sense of self she once had. Her primary hope is to find ways to integrate the traumatic memories without them overshadowing her identity and relationships.
